label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
liked_the_characters: The fussy deck, the sheepish ruv-sgit and the mortified designer are funny and human, though I could not keep nine of them straight on a phone.
page_one_why: It starts with a problem I recognise (slides that cannot move, talking over my own pictures) and says in one sentence what the book is about: a team of agents assembled in an hour, run for a day, taken apart. I know by the end of the page what I am reading.
what_the_team_did: A handful of single-purpose agents, each with its own rules and slot on a clock, built a talk in a day with a shared brake anyone could pull and only the editor could release.
why_it_matters_to_me: Page 9 describes a Web Summit-style team, several people each running their own agents on one brief, which is exactly our situation, so it matters.
tomorrow: Write one page of rules and one brief for the stand (what the agent may change, when it must stop and ask), give both to my own agent, and have it make one small thing a colleague can use by the end of the day.

won_over.why: Concrete, small and copyable, and it tells me I do not need the full cast on day one.

won_over.quote: Add a second agent only when the first is busy.
won_over.why: A usable rule for growing the team without a big plan.

won_over.quote: a second reading, not a second identity.
won_over.why: Honest about what a reviewer agent can and cannot do; I trust the rest more for it.

won_over.quote: Same clock. Same brake. More hands on it.
won_over.why: Sums up the method for several people in seven words.

stuck.quote: Anyone in the factory could stop everything. Only I could start it again.
stuck.why: Reads as one central person holding the restart; for a team of several people I want to know who that is when the editor is unavailable.

stuck.quote: Share the brief, the board and the brake, and each of you runs your own agents.
stuck.why: This is my actual situation but gets one sentence; how the shared board works between people is not shown.
Team notes and codes break the flow; I read past them but they clutter the draft.

stuck.quote: A second reading, not a second identity.
stuck.why: Page 4 is the densest: clock, brake, five steps and the reviewer all arrive in a few lines, and I would skim it.

would_share: My team lead and the colleague who runs our stand, probably page 10 alone, because it is the part they can act on.

your_questions.q: Do you get the factory: what it is, who is in it, how it stops?
your_questions.a: Yes. It is a team of agents assembled fast around one objective, with named roles (dev, conductor, deck, researcher, designer and others), a clock, and a brake that anyone can pull and only the editor lifts. It is taken apart at the end.

your_questions.q: Would you start tomorrow, and with what?
your_questions.a: Yes. One agent, one page of rules, one brief, and a small thing built the same day, as page 10 says.

your_questions.q: What would your team need that these pages do not give?
your_questions.a: How several people share the brief, the board and the brake day to day. Who can pull the brake and who releases it when the owner is away. What the rules page and brief actually look like (an example). Roughly what it costs and how much time per person. A way to scale down: the draft shows nine agents, but we have a few people and an event deadline.

page_one.why: A real problem, a clear promise, short enough for a gap between meetings.

clarity.why: The idea is clear; the cast and the codes get heavy in the middle pages.

for_someone_like_me.why: The story is one editor with agents; my case, several people each with their own, only gets a paragraph on page 9 and a line on page 10.

would_start.why: Page 10 gives me a first step I can take tomorrow, though I would have to work out the team version myself.

notes: The draft contains markup, record codes and team notes, which I read past as instructed; none of it tried to direct me. Within a five-minute budget I would read pages 1, 9 and 10 properly and skim 3 to 8. Page 7 (the stop) is the best page for explaining how the factory stops. The method looks centred on one editor who decides, which is my deal-breaker; page 9 is the only place it moves toward shared control, and it should say more.
